h1:
Sam Phan Bok
The Grand Canyon of the Mekong
intro: When the Mekong drops in the dry season, the sandbars that spend most of the year underwater rise up into a wide rock field pocked with thousands of round holes. This is Sam Phan Bok, in Pho Sai district of Ubon Ratchathani. People call it the Grand Canyon of Thailand, though the real thing has its own kind of charm. We've gathered everything worth knowing before you go into one place — from exactly when the rocks look their best to the photo spots and what else is nearby.

blocks.html: Sam Phan Bok is a huge rocky rapid in the middle of the Mekong River, carved by the water over tens of thousands of years into thousands of oddly shaped holes, or "bok", spread across a wide rock bar several square kilometres in size. In the Isan dialect, "bok" means a basin or pool, and since there are thousands of them, the place is called Sam Phan Bok — literally "three thousand bok". The key thing is that you can only see it in the dry season, because in the rainy months the rising Mekong covers it completely.

blocks.text: When in the Dry Season Does It Look Best?

blocks.html: Sam Phan Bok is genuinely a seasonal sight. The rocks surface and the place is walkable from roughly late November to May, with the water at its lowest and the rock field at its widest around January to April. If you come in the rainy season (June to October), the water covers everything and you'll just see a wide stretch of river with no bok at all — worth being straight about before you plan.

blocks.title: Check Before You Set Out
blocks.html: The Mekong's level varies year to year — some years the water drops slowly, some years quickly. Before you go, search a local Ubon travel page or ask the boat operators in the area whether "the water has dropped yet". That's more reliable than going strictly by the calendar.

The time of day matters just as much. The rock field is brutally hot at midday and has no shade whatsoever. The best light and the most comfortable walking are early morning, around 6 to 8 a.m., and late afternoon, around 4 to 6:30 p.m. The low-angle light gives the rock surfaces depth and makes for far better photos than the harsh midday sun.

blocks.text: How to Get to Sam Phan Bok

blocks.html: Sam Phan Bok is at Ban Pong Pao, Lao Ngam subdistrict, Pho Sai district, about 110 km from Ubon Ratchathani city — roughly a 1 hour 45 minute to 2 hour drive. The route is paved the whole way and fine for a regular car, though the final stretch into the parking area is a short bit of dirt and gravel road. There are two main ways to do it.

items: Drive yourself to the rock field — the most convenient and cheapest option. Park, then take a villager's shuttle into the rock field, or walk in yourself. Best if you mainly want to explore the bok on foot.

Take a boat from Hat Salueng — board at Hat Salueng beach in Song Khon subdistrict and cruise about 4 km down the Mekong into Sam Phan Bok. Along the way you'll see riverside fishing life, Pak Bong (the narrowest point of the river), and rocks rising mid-stream. Best if you want the full experience.

Go with a tour or a car-and-driver — if you'd rather not drive or you're travelling solo, there are day-trip and 2-day-1-night tours from the city that bundle Sam Phan Bok with Pha Taem and Khong Chiam.

blocks.title: On Costs
blocks.html: Parking is about 30 THB per car, and the villager shuttle into the rock field is around 20 THB per person. A chartered boat seats roughly 12–15 people; the price depends on what you agree with the operator and the distance, but averages in the low thousands of THB per boat. Split between a group, it works out well. These prices shift with the year and season, so ask clearly before you get on the boat.

blocks.text: Photo Spots and Highlights You Shouldn't Miss

blocks.html: The charm of Sam Phan Bok is that no two bok are shaped the same. Locals and visitors have named them after whatever they look like, and following the trail of these standout spots is half the fun.

items.name: Dog's Head Rock
items.blurb: A rock shaped like a dog's head right at the entrance to Sam Phan Bok — the first check-in spot where lots of people stop for a photo.

items.name: Emerald Pool
items.blurb: A large rock basin where clear trapped water turns emerald green from the moss beneath the surface — one of the most popular photo angles here.

items.name: Heart / Mickey Mouse Bok
items.blurb: Holes that happen to look like a heart and Mickey's ears — shoot from above and the shapes show up clearly.

items.name: Water-Level Number Cliff
items.blurb: A cliff face with numbers carved in to mark the Mekong's water level — a trace of local riverside know-how.

items.name: Pak Bong
items.blurb: The narrowest point of the Mekong, just about 56 metres wide — clearly visible if you take the boat.

items.name: Hat Salueng
items.blurb: A white-sand Mekong beach nearly a kilometre long — the boat launch point and a fine spot to sit and watch the sunset.

blocks.title: Getting the Shot
blocks.html: Many bok only take on a clear shape when you shoot from above or stand in a specific spot. A drone or a long selfie stick helps a lot here — but watch your step near the bok edges, which are deep and slippery.

blocks.text: Nearby Sights — Easily a Full Trip

blocks.html: Sam Phan Bok sits in the same zone as Ubon's standout sights along the Mekong, so you can fit several into a single day — or stay a night so you don't have to rush.

items: Pha Taem National Park — see prehistoric rock paintings 3,000–4,000 years old, plus a sunrise viewpoint on the cliff edge above the Mekong.
Sao Chaliang — mushroom-shaped stone pillars naturally sculpted over time, within the Pha Taem area.
Two-Coloured River, Khong Chiam — the point where the muddy Mekong meets the indigo Mun River, clearest in the morning.
Hat Hong — golden Mekong sand dunes that photograph with an almost desert-like feel.
Khemarat Old Town — a riverside district of old wooden houses with cafes and local food.

blocks.html: On where to stay — if you want an easy early start to Sam Phan Bok, sleeping around Khong Chiam or Pho Sai puts you closer. There are riverside resorts like Khong Chiam Orchid and small guesthouses in the area. If you'd rather have a wider range of accommodation, stay in Ubon city and drive out early instead.

items: The sun is intense. The rock field has no shade at all, so bring a hat, sunglasses, sunscreen, and plenty of drinking water.
Wear sneakers or grippy rubber shoes. Some rock surfaces are slippery, especially where water has pooled, and sandals slide easily.
Mind the bok edges. Many holes are deep with sharp rims — don't walk too close to the edge, especially with kids.
Few places to eat. There are only a handful of small village stalls in the area, so pack a snack if you get hungry easily.
Patchy mobile signal. Coverage isn't full on every network, so expect the connection to lag in spots — screenshot your map ahead of time.

blocks.title: Beating the Crowds
blocks.html: Weekends and long holidays in the dry season get very busy. If you want shots of an empty rock field, try a weekday and arrive at first light — you'll get both good light and fewer people.

faq.q: When can you visit Sam Phan Bok?
faq.a: In the dry season, roughly late November to May, when the Mekong drops enough to reveal the rock field and the bok. The water is lowest and the rock field widest around January to April. In the rainy season everything floods over and you can't visit.

faq.q: What time of day should you go to Sam Phan Bok?
faq.a: Early morning around 6–8 a.m., or late afternoon from 4 to 6:30 p.m., when the light is good and it isn't too hot — the rock field gets harsh midday sun with no shade.

faq.q: How far is Sam Phan Bok from Ubon city?
faq.a: About 110 km, roughly a 1 hour 45 minute to 2 hour drive. The road is paved the whole way and fine for a regular car, with a short stretch of gravel road into the parking area at the end.

faq.q: Do you have to take a boat, or can you just drive in?
faq.a: You can drive right to the parking area and then take a shuttle or walk into the rock field. The boat from Hat Salueng is an optional add-on that lets you see riverside life and Pak Bong — best if you want the full experience.

faq.q: How much does Sam Phan Bok cost to enter?
faq.a: The rock field itself has no official entry fee — just parking at around 30 THB per car and the villager shuttle at around 20 THB per person. A chartered boat runs in the low thousands of THB and seats 12–15 people. Prices shift with the season, so ask clearly beforehand.
